chunks: And from him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd and Ibn Abi Najran, both of them, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said:

I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Ali (peace be upon him) ruled regarding one who swore an oath by the oath of Sabr to a man from the People of the Book, that he should swear by his book and his religion.'

key_terms.أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ: People of the Book (Christians and Jews)
key_terms.بِيَمِينِ صَبْرٍ: By the oath of Sabr (referring to a specific oath type or context)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for swearing an oath by a man from the People of the Book in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential principle of *istihsan* (juridical preference) in oaths, where Imam Ali (AS) ruled that a person from the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*) should swear by their own scripture and religion rather than adopting a specific Islamic formula like the 'oath of Sabr.' This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly view that validity in oaths depends on the sincerity and identity of the swearer, preserving the integrity of their religious context while ensuring legal enforceability. It highlights the flexibility in Islamic jurisprudence to accommodate non-Muslims in legal proceedings without compromising the core tenets of the oath.
